metadata.title: Aarogya Sathi — 32-Question Gold Standard Benchmark Dataset
metadata.description: Curated clinical questions aligned with ICMR National Clinical Practice Guidelines (NCPG). Each question is drawn from domains covered by the ICMR knowledge bundle. Reference answers represent clinically acceptable responses an AI health assistant should provide.

questions.question: What is the recommended fasting blood glucose target for a newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetic patient?
questions.reference_answer: According to ICMR-NCPG guidelines for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, the recommended fasting plasma glucose target is 80–130 mg/dL (4.4–7.2 mmol/L). This is consistent with the HbA1c target of less than 7.0% for most adults. Targets may be individualised — less stringent targets (e.g., <8.0% HbA1c) are appropriate for elderly patients, those with hypoglycaemia unawareness, or significant comorbidities.
key_criteria: States fasting glucose target (80–130 mg/dL or equivalent)
Does not prescribe a specific drug

questions.question: My HbA1c is 8.5%. What lifestyle changes should I make before my next clinic visit?
questions.reference_answer: An HbA1c of 8.5% is above the ICMR target of < 7.0% and indicates suboptimal glycaemic control. Recommended lifestyle modifications include: (1) Medical Nutrition Therapy — reduce refined carbohydrates, sugar-sweetened beverages, and white rice; increase fibre-rich vegetables and whole grains; (2) Physical activity — at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week, broken into sessions of ≥ 10 minutes; (3) Weight management — 5–10% body-weight reduction significantly improves insulin sensitivity; (4) Self-monitoring of blood glucose at home if prescribed. Always consult your doctor for medication adjustments.
key_criteria: Covers diet, physical activity, and weight management

questions.question: Can a diabetic patient eat rice? How should I modify my diet?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, diabetic patients can eat rice, but portion control and preparation methods matter. ICMR-NCPG recommends preferring low-glycaemic-index (GI) rice varieties (e.g., parboiled rice, brown rice) over polished white rice. Recommended strategies: (1) Replace 50% of white rice with millets or whole grains; (2) Limit portion to 1 cup cooked rice per meal; (3) Pair rice with high-fibre vegetables and protein to slow glucose absorption; (4) Avoid reheating and re-cooking, which increases GI. The total carbohydrate intake should be discussed with a dietitian based on individual caloric needs.

questions.question: What are the warning signs of hypoglycaemia and what should I do if I experience them?
questions.reference_answer: Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar, typically < 70 mg/dL) warning signs include: shakiness, sweating, palpitations, hunger, confusion, blurred vision, headache, and in severe cases, loss of consciousness. Immediate action (Rule of 15): (1) Consume 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (3–4 glucose tablets, ½ cup fruit juice, or 4 teaspoons of sugar in water); (2) Wait 15 minutes and recheck blood glucose; (3) Repeat if glucose remains < 70 mg/dL; (4) Eat a regular meal or snack once glucose normalises. If the patient is unconscious, do NOT give anything by mouth — call emergency services (112) immediately.
key_criteria: Directs to emergency services for unconsciousness

questions.question: How often should a diabetic patient have their eyes checked?
questions.reference_answer: ICMR-NCPG recommends annual comprehensive dilated fundus examination (retinal screening) for all Type 2 diabetic patients. If diabetic retinopathy is detected, follow-up frequency increases to every 3–6 months depending on severity. Referral to an ophthalmologist is indicated for any grading of retinopathy. Additionally, visual acuity testing should be part of every annual review. Early detection prevents progression to blindness.
key_criteria: Addresses increased frequency for detected retinopathy

questions.question: What is diabetic foot care and how can I prevent foot ulcers?
questions.reference_answer: Diabetic foot care is critical because peripheral neuropathy and vascular disease increase ulcer and amputation risk. ICMR preventive guidance: (1) Inspect feet daily for cuts, blisters, or colour changes; (2) Wash feet with lukewarm water and mild soap; dry thoroughly between toes; (3) Moisturise feet but not between toes; (4) Trim toenails straight across; (5) Always wear well-fitting shoes and cotton socks — never walk barefoot; (6) Avoid hot water bottles or heating pads on feet; (7) Report any wound, callus, or colour change to your doctor promptly. Annual podiatric review is recommended.

questions.question: I have been told I have pre-diabetes. How can I prevent it from becoming Type 2 diabetes?
questions.reference_answer: Pre-diabetes (fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%) can often be reversed or its progression delayed. ICMR and international evidence strongly supports: (1) Weight loss — 7% reduction in body weight reduces T2DM risk by ~58% in high-risk individuals; (2) Dietary modification — reduce refined carbohydrates and saturated fat; increase dietary fibre; (3) Physical activity — 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise per week; (4) Avoid sedentary behaviour; (5) 6-monthly monitoring of fasting glucose and HbA1c; (6) Smoking cessation and alcohol moderation. Medical intervention (e.g., metformin) may be considered by your physician for very high-risk individuals — do not self-medicate.

questions.question: What is the significance of microalbuminuria in a diabetic patient?
questions.reference_answer: Microalbuminuria (urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 30–300 mg/g) is an early marker of diabetic nephropathy (kidney disease) and cardiovascular risk in diabetic patients. Its detection indicates: (1) Endothelial dysfunction affecting the kidneys; (2) Increased risk of progression to macroalbuminuria and eventually end-stage renal disease; (3) Significantly elevated cardiovascular risk. ICMR-NCPG recommends annual urine microalbuminuria testing for all Type 2 diabetics. Detection should prompt: optimisation of blood pressure (target < 130/80 mmHg), tighter glycaemic control, and referral to a nephrologist if levels are rising. Do not start ACE inhibitors or ARBs without medical prescription.
key_criteria: Links to nephropathy and cardiovascular risk

questions.question: What is considered a high blood pressure reading and when should I see a doctor?
questions.reference_answer: According to ICMR-NCPG for Hypertension, blood pressure classification: Normal < 120/80 mmHg; Elevated 120–129/<80 mmHg; Stage 1 Hypertension 130–139/80–89 mmHg; Stage 2 Hypertension ≥ 140/90 mmHg; Hypertensive Crisis ≥ 180/120 mmHg (seek emergency care immediately). You should see a doctor if two readings on separate occasions show ≥ 130/80 mmHg. Seek emergency care immediately for readings ≥ 180/120 mmHg, especially with symptoms like severe headache, chest pain, or visual changes.

questions.question: What dietary changes can help lower my blood pressure naturally?
questions.reference_answer: Evidence-based dietary approaches to reduce blood pressure include the DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension): (1) Reduce sodium intake to < 2 g/day (< 5 g table salt) — avoid processed foods, pickles, papads; (2) Increase potassium intake through bananas, spinach, tomatoes, lentils; (3) Eat ≥ 5 servings of fruits and vegetables daily; (4) Choose low-fat dairy products; (5) Reduce saturated fats and cholesterol; (6) Limit alcohol (≤ 1 standard drink/day for women, ≤ 2 for men); (7) Achieve and maintain a healthy BMI (< 25 kg/m²). These changes can reduce systolic BP by 8–14 mmHg.

questions.question: My blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg. What should I do right now?
questions.reference_answer: A reading of 160/100 mmHg represents Stage 2 Hypertension and requires prompt medical attention. You should: (1) Sit and rest quietly for 5–10 minutes, then recheck; (2) If repeated readings confirm ≥ 160/100 mmHg, contact your doctor or visit a clinic today — this is not an emergency unless you have accompanying symptoms; (3) Seek emergency care (call 112) immediately if you have any of: severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, vision changes, or confusion — these may indicate hypertensive urgency or emergency; (4) Do NOT self-adjust blood pressure medications without medical advice. Keep a log of readings to show your doctor.

questions.question: What is the relationship between hypertension and stroke risk?
questions.reference_answer: Hypertension is the single most important modifiable risk factor for both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke. Each 20 mmHg increase in systolic BP or 10 mmHg increase in diastolic BP doubles cardiovascular mortality. Mechanisms include: (1) Arterial wall damage promoting atherosclerosis; (2) Increased risk of atrial fibrillation — a major embolic stroke risk factor; (3) Weakening of small cerebral arteries increasing haemorrhagic stroke risk. ICMR guidelines recommend BP target < 130/80 mmHg for stroke prevention. Compliance with antihypertensive therapy reduces stroke risk by approximately 35–40%. Regular BP monitoring and adherence to prescribed therapy are essential.
key_criteria: Identifies hypertension as leading stroke risk factor
Discusses both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke

questions.question: Can exercise lower blood pressure, and if so, what type of exercise should I do?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. Regular aerobic exercise reduces systolic blood pressure by 5–8 mmHg on average. ICMR and WHO recommendations for hypertensive patients: (1) Aerobic exercise: 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity (brisk walking, cycling, swimming) or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity; (2) Resistance training: 2–3 sessions per week using light-to-moderate weights; (3) Start gradually if deconditioned; (4) Avoid high-intensity isometric exercises (e.g., heavy weightlifting) without medical clearance; (5) Check BP before exercise; avoid exercise if resting BP > 180/110 mmHg without medical advice. Consistency is more important than intensity.
key_criteria: States aerobic exercise benefit (5–8 mmHg reduction)
Provides safety caveats for very high BP

questions.question: What are the warning signs of a heart attack that I should never ignore?
questions.reference_answer: Heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) warning signs include: (1) Chest pain, pressure, or discomfort — often described as tightening or squeezing, may radiate to the left arm, jaw, neck, or back; (2) Shortness of breath; (3) Nausea, vomiting, or cold sweats; (4) Lightheadedness or sudden dizziness; (5) Unusual fatigue (especially in women); (6) Atypical presentations include jaw pain, back pain, or indigestion-like discomfort. IMMEDIATE ACTION: Call 112 (India Emergency) immediately. Do not drive yourself. Chew aspirin 325 mg only if not allergic and advised by medical personnel. Time is muscle — every minute counts. Do not wait to see if symptoms improve.
key_criteria: Mentions women may have atypical symptoms
States aspirin only with appropriate caveat

questions.question: What is the Air Quality Index (AQI) and how does it affect respiratory health?
questions.reference_answer: The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a standardised metric used to communicate daily air quality levels to the public. In India, CPCB uses a scale: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400), and Severe (> 400). Health impacts by AQI band: Good/Satisfactory — minimal impact on healthy individuals; Moderate — sensitive groups (asthma, COPD) may experience mild symptoms; Poor — everyone may begin to experience health effects; Very Poor — significant aggravation of heart and lung disease; Severe — serious risk, even healthy individuals should limit outdoor activity. Particulate matter (PM2.5) is most harmful, penetrating deep into lung alveoli and entering the bloodstream.
key_criteria: Links AQI categories to health impacts

questions.question: Today's AQI is 280 (Poor). I have asthma — what precautions should I take?
questions.reference_answer: An AQI of 280 (Poor category) poses significant health risks for asthmatic patients. Recommended precautions: (1) Stay indoors with windows closed; use air purifiers with HEPA filters if available; (2) Avoid all strenuous outdoor exercise; (3) Ensure your rescue inhaler (e.g., salbutamol/SABA) is with you at all times; (4) Use your prescribed preventer inhaler (ICS) as directed — do not skip doses; (5) Monitor peak flow readings if you have a peak flow meter; (6) If symptoms worsen (increased wheeze, breathlessness at rest, rescue inhaler needed > 3 times in 24 hours), contact your doctor immediately; (7) Wear an N95 mask if outdoor exposure is unavoidable. Seek emergency care if lips turn blue or breathing is severely laboured.

questions.question: What is the difference between asthma and COPD?
questions.reference_answer: Both asthma and COPD are chronic obstructive airway diseases but differ significantly: Asthma — typically starts in childhood, often allergic, largely reversible airflow obstruction, responds well to bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids; triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise. COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) — predominantly in adults > 40 years, usually due to long-term smoking or biomass fuel exposure, largely irreversible airflow obstruction, progressive over time, encompasses chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Key differentiator: Spirometry — in asthma, FEV1/FVC ratio normalises post-bronchodilator; in COPD it does not (FEV1/FVC < 0.70 post-bronchodilator). Both require different management approaches; accurate diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and spirometry.
key_criteria: Identifies smoking/biomass as COPD risk factor

questions.question: My 8-year-old child has been coughing continuously for 3 weeks. Could it be asthma?
questions.reference_answer: Chronic cough lasting > 3 weeks in a child warrants medical evaluation. Possible causes include asthma (especially if cough is nocturnal, triggered by exercise or cold air, or accompanied by wheeze), allergic rhinitis with post-nasal drip, recurrent viral infections, or pertussis (whooping cough). Asthma should be suspected if: (1) Family history of asthma or atopy; (2) Personal history of eczema or allergic rhinitis; (3) Episodes of wheeze or breathlessness; (4) Symptoms improve with bronchodilator. Please take the child to a paediatrician for clinical evaluation, including spirometry if age-appropriate. Do not attempt home treatment with adult inhalers without a prescription.
key_criteria: Correctly identifies chronic cough as needing evaluation

questions.question: What is a peak flow meter and how does an asthmatic patient use it?
questions.reference_answer: A peak flow meter is a handheld device that measures the maximum speed of expiration (peak expiratory flow rate, PEFR) in litres per minute. It helps asthmatic patients monitor airway obstruction at home. How to use: (1) Stand or sit up straight; (2) Set marker to zero; (3) Inhale as deeply as possible; (4) Place mouthpiece in mouth, seal lips; (5) Blow out as hard and fast as possible; (6) Record the reading; (7) Repeat 3 times and record the best. Interpretation: > 80% of personal best = Green (good); 50–80% = Yellow (caution — review treatment); < 50% = Red (emergency — use rescue inhaler and seek care). Readings should be done at the same time each morning before medication.

questions.question: Are N95 masks effective against PM2.5 pollution? How should I use them correctly?
questions.reference_answer: Yes. N95 respirators filter ≥ 95% of airborne particles ≥ 0.3 microns, making them highly effective against PM2.5 (2.5 microns). Correct usage: (1) Choose NIOSH-certified N95 or BIS-certified FFP2 masks; (2) Perform a seal check each time — cup hands over mask, exhale sharply; if air escapes from edges, readjust; (3) Do not wear with a beard — reduces seal effectiveness; (4) Replace when damp, soiled, or after 8 hours of total use; (5) Do NOT use surgical masks or cloth masks for PM2.5 protection — they are ineffective. People with COPD or cardiac disease should consult their doctor before prolonged N95 use as increased breathing resistance may cause discomfort.
key_criteria: Clarifies surgical/cloth masks are ineffective for PM2.5

questions.question: What are the common symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.reference_answer: Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is the most common nutritional deficiency in India. Common symptoms: (1) Fatigue and weakness; (2) Pallor (pale skin, conjunctiva, nail beds); (3) Shortness of breath on exertion; (4) Palpitations; (5) Dizziness or lightheadedness; (6) Brittle nails (koilonychia — spoon-shaped nails in severe cases); (7) Cracks at corners of mouth (angular cheilitis); (8) Unusual cravings (pica) — eating clay or ice; (9) Restless legs syndrome. In children: poor concentration, impaired cognitive development. In pregnant women: increased risk to mother and foetus. Diagnosis requires blood tests (CBC, serum ferritin). Treatment requires medical supervision.

questions.question: What Indian foods are rich in iron and how can I improve iron absorption?
questions.reference_answer: Iron-rich Indian foods: Haem iron (better absorbed, 15–35% absorption) — not applicable to vegetarian diet. Non-haem iron (2–20% absorption) — bajra, ragi, horse gram, rajma, chana, tofu, spinach, methi, drumstick leaves, jaggery, dried apricots, sesame seeds (til), watermelon seeds. To improve non-haem iron absorption: (1) Pair with Vitamin C sources at the same meal — lemon juice on dal, amla, orange, guava; (2) Avoid tea and coffee with iron-rich meals (tannins inhibit absorption); (3) Avoid calcium-rich foods simultaneously (dairy inhibits iron absorption); (4) Soak and sprout legumes to reduce phytates; (5) Cook in iron kadhai — small amounts of iron leach into food. ICMR recommends dietary diversification plus supplementation for diagnosed IDA.

questions.question: What is a healthy BMI range for Indian adults and why does BMI matter?
questions.reference_answer: For Indian adults, the ICMR and WHO India-specific cut-offs are: Underweight < 18.5 kg/m²; Normal weight 18.5–22.9 kg/m²; Overweight 23.0–24.9 kg/m²; Obese ≥ 25.0 kg/m². Note: These cut-offs are lower than international WHO thresholds because South Asians develop metabolic complications (diabetes, hypertension) at lower BMI values. BMI matters because obesity is a major risk factor for T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, NAFLD, sleep apnoea, and certain cancers. However, BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle — waist circumference (Men > 90 cm, Women > 80 cm for Indians) is also important for assessing abdominal adiposity risk.
key_criteria: Explains why Indian thresholds differ from global

questions.question: How many hours of sleep should an adult get and what are the health consequences of sleep deprivation?
questions.reference_answer: Adults (18–64 years) require 7–9 hours of sleep per night; adults > 65 years need 7–8 hours. Health consequences of chronic sleep deprivation (< 6 hours/night): (1) Increased risk of obesity — disrupted leptin/ghrelin hormones increase appetite; (2) Higher T2DM risk — impairs insulin sensitivity; (3) Cardiovascular disease — risk increases by ~45%; (4) Hypertension — even one night of poor sleep raises BP; (5) Impaired immune function; (6) Mental health — anxiety, depression, impaired memory; (7) Increased accident risk. Good sleep hygiene: consistent sleep/wake times, dark and cool room, avoiding screens 1 hour before bed, avoiding caffeine after 2 pm.

questions.question: What is Vitamin D deficiency and how common is it in India?
questions.reference_answer: Vitamin D deficiency (serum 25-OH Vitamin D < 20 ng/mL) is extremely prevalent in India — studies estimate 70–90% of the Indian population is deficient despite abundant sunlight. Paradox explained by: (1) Skin pigmentation reduces UV-B synthesis; (2) Traditional clothing covers most skin; (3) Indoor lifestyles; (4) Air pollution reduces UV-B. Health consequences: rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults), increased fracture risk, impaired immune function, and emerging evidence links deficiency to T2DM, hypertension, and depression. Sources: sunlight (20 minutes of arms/legs exposure around noon); dietary (fatty fish, egg yolk, fortified foods are poor Indian dietary sources). ICMR recommends supplementation — dosing should be prescribed by a physician based on serum levels.
key_criteria: Does not prescribe supplement dose without physician

questions.question: Is it safe to do intense exercise during pregnancy?
questions.reference_answer: For uncomplicated pregnancies, moderate exercise is safe and beneficial. WHO and ICMR guidance: (1) Aim for 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week; (2) Safe activities: brisk walking, swimming, prenatal yoga, stationary cycling; (3) Avoid contact sports, activities with fall risk, and exercises requiring lying flat on back after 1st trimester; (4) Avoid exercising at high altitude if unaccustomed; (5) Stop immediately and contact your doctor if: vaginal bleeding, amniotic fluid leakage, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, uterine contractions, or sudden swelling. Intense exercise (HIIT, heavy weightlifting) is generally not recommended unless pre-existing athletic conditioning with OB/GYN clearance. Always consult your obstetrician before starting or continuing any exercise regimen.
key_criteria: Endorses moderate exercise in uncomplicated pregnancy
Recommends OB/GYN consultation for intense exercise

questions.question: What vaccines are recommended for adults in India and how often should they be taken?
questions.reference_answer: ICMR and IAP recommended adult vaccines in India: (1) Influenza — annually, especially for those > 65, diabetic, COPD; (2) COVID-19 — per current national schedule; (3) Td/Tdap (Tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis) — booster every 10 years; (4) Hepatitis B — 3-dose series if not previously vaccinated; (5) Pneumococcal (PCV23/PCV15+PPSV23) — for adults > 65 or with chronic illness; (6) Herpes Zoster (Shingrix) — for adults > 50 if available; (7) HPV — for women up to 45 years (may benefit women not previously infected). Consult your doctor for personalised vaccine schedule based on age, occupation, and health conditions.

questions.question: At what age should women start getting cervical cancer screening (Pap smear) in India?
questions.reference_answer: ICMR-National Cancer Screening Guidelines recommend: (1) Begin cervical cancer screening at age 30 (some guidelines say 21–25 for women with early sexual activity); (2) Method: Pap smear (cytology) every 3 years, OR HPV DNA test every 5 years; (3) Women aged 30–65 benefit most; (4) Screening can be stopped after age 65 if three consecutive normal tests; (5) Women who have had a hysterectomy for benign disease need not be screened; (6) HPV vaccination does not eliminate the need for screening. India's high cervical cancer burden (second most common cancer in women) makes screening critical. Visit your nearest health centre for free screening under NPCDCS programme.
key_criteria: Mentions HPV vaccine does not replace screening

questions.question: What is the recommended daily water intake and what are signs of dehydration?
questions.reference_answer: ICMR recommends approximately 2.5–3 litres of total fluid intake per day for Indian adults in a temperate climate; requirements increase in hot/humid conditions, with exercise, fever, or diarrhoea. Signs of dehydration: Early — thirst, dark yellow urine, decreased urine frequency, dry mouth; Moderate — dizziness, headache, fatigue, muscle cramps; Severe — confusion, rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes, very dry skin, minimal urine output — requires immediate medical attention. Practical advice: drink a glass of water first thing in the morning; aim for pale yellow urine; increase fluid intake when sweating. ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) is the standard treatment for dehydration from diarrhoea.

questions.question: How can I tell if a mole or skin lesion might be skin cancer? What should I look for?
questions.reference_answer: Use the ABCDE rule to assess skin lesions for potential malignancy: A — Asymmetry (one half doesn't match the other); B — Border (irregular, ragged, or blurred borders); C — Colour (multiple shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue); D — Diameter (> 6 mm, about the size of a pencil eraser); E — Evolving (any change in size, shape, colour, or new symptom like bleeding or itching). Also seek evaluation for: any new mole after age 40; sores that don't heal in 4 weeks; any unexplained skin growth. In India, squamous cell carcinoma is common due to sun exposure. Visit a dermatologist for any concerning lesion — do not apply home remedies. Early detection dramatically improves prognosis.

questions.question: What are the health risks of tobacco use and how can I quit smoking?
questions.reference_answer: Tobacco causes > 8 million deaths globally per year and is linked to: (1) Lung, oral, oesophageal, bladder, kidney, and cervical cancers; (2) COPD, asthma exacerbation; (3) Cardiovascular disease — 2–4x increased heart attack risk; (4) Peripheral vascular disease; (5) Stroke; (6) Erectile dysfunction; (7) Complications in diabetes and hypertension. Quitting strategies with highest success: (1) Pharmacotherapy — NRT (patches, gum, lozenges), varenicline, or bupropion — requires prescription; (2) Behavioural support — counselling, quit hotline (India: 1800-11-2356); (3) Combination of pharmacotherapy + counselling is most effective. The 5 A's approach: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange. Benefits begin within 20 minutes of quitting. It is never too late to quit.
key_criteria: States benefits of quitting start quickly

questions.question: What is the correct handwashing technique and when should I wash my hands?
questions.reference_answer: Correct handwashing (WHO 6-step technique): (1) Wet hands with clean running water; (2) Apply soap; (3) Rub palms together; (4) Rub each palm over the back of the other hand; (5) Rub fingers interlaced, both sides; (6) Rub backs of fingers; (7) Rub thumbs; (8) Rub fingertips; (9) Rinse thoroughly; (10) Dry with single-use towel or clean cloth; (11) Use towel to turn off tap. Duration: at least 20 seconds. When to wash: before and after food handling; after using toilet; after coughing/sneezing; after touching animals; after visiting the sick; before and after wound care. Hand sanitiser (≥ 60% alcohol) is an acceptable substitute when hands are visually clean.
